cards.title: Nvidia loses its founder CEO overnight; the CFO steps in

visual.label: Nvidia's close on Thursday, after a double-digit fall at the open

cards.what: Jensen Huang resigned as CEO and director with immediate effect. CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO, and the board named its first chair.
cards.why: Key-person risk has landed at AI's most important supplier. Every large AI plan depends on its chips arriving on schedule.
cards.say: Which of our AI commitments assume one supplier's roadmap holds, and what is plan B?
deeper: Nvidia's board said on 12 November that Jensen Huang had stepped down as president, chief executive and board member. The exit came days after the board opened an investigation into news reports about his conduct. Colette Kress keeps the CFO role while acting as interim chief executive. Harvey Jones, a director since 1993, becomes the first chair the board has had. A search will consider internal and external candidates.

The board said operations, customer commitments and the product roadmap continue without interruption. The first test is close: third-quarter results are due on 17 November. Watch whether large customers repeat that message, and whether the search is given a deadline.

cards.title: Oil jumps to $95.82 as hopes of an Iran deal fade

visual.label: Brent crude at Thursday's settle, up 3.3% in one day

cards.what: Brent rose $3.06 after President Trump said no Iran deal was needed and Houthi forces claimed strikes on Saudi energy sites.
cards.why: India imports most of its oil. Dearer crude and a weaker rupee raise costs, inflation risk and pressure on budgets.
cards.say: Have our 2027 cost plans been tested at $100 oil and a 95 rupee?
deeper: Oil had been falling this month on hopes that the US-Iran conflict was winding down. Thursday reversed part of that. Crude dropped early, then climbed after a social media post from President Trump saying Washington did not need a deal. Yemen's Houthis then said they had hit a pipeline pumping station, a facility at Yanbu and an Aramco building. Saudi Arabia's coalition said it destroyed two drones.

Both oil benchmarks were still down about 2.5% for the week, and US stockpiles rose. The swing matters more than the level: energy costs are again being set by headlines. In India the rupee closed at 94.04 to the dollar, 33 paise weaker.

cards.title: Rate rises are back: markets see an ECB hike in December

visual.label: chance markets give a quarter-point ECB rise in December

cards.what: Traders price an 80% chance that the ECB lifts its deposit rate to 2.75% on 17 December. Bets on a US rise are growing too.
cards.why: Money is getting dearer again. Business cases approved at last year's rates may no longer clear the bar.
cards.say: Which approved programmes still pay back if the cost of capital rises one point?
deeper: A Reuters poll published on 12 November found most economists expect one final ECB rise next month. More than a third expect another in early 2027. Forecasts for euro zone inflation were raised to 3.1% this year and 2.8% next year, well above the 2% target, with energy the main driver.

The US is moving the same way. Higher than expected October inflation pushed up Treasury yields and bets on a Federal Reserve rise, and the dollar strengthened. For companies, the practical effect is a higher hurdle rate for investment and a stronger dollar on import bills.

cards.title: Agents are live at 71% of firms; only 30% run alone

visual.title: Share of enterprise leaders, Zapier survey

cards.what: A Zapier survey of 513 enterprise leaders found 71% have agents in production. Only 30% say agents finish most tasks without human help.
cards.why: Adoption is settled. Return, risk and job design are decided in the gap between deployed and autonomous.
cards.say: How many of our live agents are assist, supervised or autonomous, and what evidence moves one up?
deeper: Zapier polled the leaders between 16 and 21 September and compared the answers with a similar poll a year earlier. Use or testing of agents rose from 72% to 88%. Zapier sells automation software, so the headline numbers deserve some caution. The more useful finding is the split: most firms have agents running, but people still check or complete most of the work.

That split is an operating model question, not a technology one. Each agent needs a named owner, a stated level of autonomy and a test for moving to the next level. Without that, cost is added without removing work.

sources.title: Zapier: 88% of enterprises now use or test AI agents

cards.title: JD.com takes control of MediaMarkt's parent to enter Europe through stores

visual.label: of Ceconomy now held by JD.com and its partner Convergenta

cards.what: JD.com completed its offer for Ceconomy, buying 59.8% for about €1.3 billion at €4.60 a share. Ceconomy is now a subsidiary.
cards.why: A Chinese online giant chose to buy shops, customers and local trust in Europe, not to build them slowly.
cards.say: Where could we buy distribution and trust faster than we can build it?
deeper: The deal closed on 12 November after merger, foreign investment and EU foreign subsidy clearances. JD.com's partner Convergenta keeps 25.3%, which takes the combined holding to 85.2%. Ceconomy owns the MediaMarkt and Saturn chains. Its results are now consolidated into JD.com's accounts.

The logic is a swap of strengths. JD.com brings supply chain and logistics technology. Ceconomy brings stores, customers and a familiar brand. With spending at home soft, expansion abroad carries more weight for Chinese retailers. The open question is integration: whether technology can be transferred without disturbing what local customers trust.

cards.title: GCCs now out-hire IT services firms by 60,000 a year

visual.title: People hired in a year, per recruiter Xpheno

cards.what: Recruiter Xpheno says GCCs hired 180,000 people in FY26, against 120,000 at IT services firms. A year earlier the gap was 10,000.
cards.why: Captive centres now set the talent market. Pay pressure and competition for skills rise for every employer.
cards.say: Is our talent plan benchmarked against GCCs, or still against IT services firms?
deeper: The numbers were cited by YourStory. New arrivals keep coming: Starbucks plans its first India centre in Chennai with about 800 hires, and SplashBI is opening in Hyderabad with a stated investment of over $100 million. Mid-size companies are now following the large banks and retailers.

For leaders, two things follow. Retention plans built for an IT services market are out of date. And the role of a centre is shifting from cost to capability, which changes who it reports to and how its value is measured.

cards.title: Reference class forecasting: plan from what happened to similar projects

items.label: Inside view
items.note: How will our plan unfold? Usually too hopeful.

items.label: Outside view
items.note: How did similar projects actually go?

items.label: Commit
items.note: Set the date the reference class supports.

cards.what: Forecast a project from the actual results of similar past projects, not from its own plan.
cards.why: Any date, budget or benefit case with little history and high excitement: AI programmes, migrations, new centres.
cards.say: Find five comparable projects, note how far each overran, and set the commitment at that level.
deeper: The method answers the planning fallacy, described by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky in 1979: people underestimate time, cost and risk even when they know similar work overran. Estimates are built by picturing a smooth path to done, which leaves out illness, dependencies and rework. Two smaller remedies also help: split work into small parts and estimate each, and fix when, where and how each step will happen.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Planning fallacy

cards.title: Students' worst-case guess was still shorter than the real time

visual.title: Days to finish a thesis, 1994 study

cards.what: In a 1994 study, 37 students predicted 33.9 days for a thesis. They took 55.5, beyond their own worst case of 48.6.
cards.why: Even a pessimistic scenario assumes the plan mostly works. Only outside data corrects it.
cards.say: What did the last five programmes like this actually take, and why would we beat them?
deeper: The study was run by Roger Buehler and colleagues. Only about 30% of students finished in the time they predicted. The Sydney Opera House shows the same pattern at scale: expected in 1963, opened in scaled-down form in 1973, at a cost of $102 million against an estimate of $7 million. The first estimate is made when least is known, yet it is often treated as a commitment.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Planning fallacy

blocks.sub: AI agents and tools: step 1 of 5

plan: What makes an agent an agent
Tools: how a model takes action
MCP: one plug for many tools

cards.title: An agent is a model that acts in a loop

items.label: Goal
items.note: A person sets the task and the limits.

items.label: Think
items.note: The model decides the next step.

items.label: Act
items.note: It calls a tool: search, database, email.

items.label: Check
items.note: It reads the result and repeats until done.

cards.what: A chatbot answers once. An agent plans, calls a tool, reads the result and repeats until the goal is met.
cards.why: Value and risk both come from the loop. Each extra step can add progress, cost or error.
cards.say: Take one process you know. List the tools an agent would need and where a person must approve.
deeper: Tools are what turn a language model from a writer into a worker. A tool is any system the model is allowed to call: a search engine, a database query, a ticketing system. The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, is an open standard introduced by Anthropic in November 2024 that gives AI applications one common way to connect to such tools and data. The next step covers how a tool call works.

sources.title: DigitalOcean: MCP 101, An Introduction to Model Context Protocol

blocks.title: Case file
blocks.sub: IBM, 1993: the break-up that was cancelled

cards.title: Gerstner kept IBM whole and made integration the product

visual.label: IBM market value in 2002, up from $29 billion in 1993

cards.what: In 1993 IBM was failing and a break-up plan was ready. New CEO Lou Gerstner cancelled it and sold integrated solutions.
cards.why: Market value rose almost sixfold in nine years. More than 100,000 jobs were cut on the way.
cards.say: Before a split or carve-out, ask what customers get only because the units work together.
deeper: Gerstner's reasoning is the useful part. Customers were struggling to assemble technology from many vendors, and IBM was one of few firms with hardware, software, services and research under one roof. Splitting it would have discarded the one advantage rivals could not copy. He also fixed execution and accountability before talking about vision. A caveat: part of the rise in value reflects the strong market of the late 1990s.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Lou Gerstner

cards.title: Conway's law: systems copy the organisation that builds them

visual.label: Melvin Conway's paper in Datamation, first rejected by Harvard Business Review

cards.what: An organisation designing a system will produce a design that mirrors its own communication structure.
cards.why: It explains why new technology on an old org chart reproduces old silos, including with AI agents.
cards.say: If we want a different system, we have to change who talks to whom first.
deeper: Conway's point was wider than software. One of his examples of a system is a public transport network. The structure of a design team limits which designs can even be considered, because some options need communication paths that do not exist. Fred Brooks named it Conway's law in The Mythical Man-Month. The practical use today: design the team around the system wanted, not the reverse.

sources.title: ACM Queue: How Do Committees Invent? and Ironies of Automation
The Morning Paper: How do committees invent?
O'Reilly, Making Software: Conway's Law

cards.title: Human in the loop
cards.what: A person must review or approve an AI system's action before it takes effect. The system waits.
cards.why: As agents gain autonomy, leaders must say where approval is required and where supervision is enough.
cards.say: Payments stay human in the loop; routine triage can move to human on the loop.
deeper: On the loop means a person supervises and can step in, but the system does not wait. Out of the loop means it acts alone. The common mistake is rubber-stamping: an approval step that nobody has time to do properly is oversight in name only.

sources.title: CASRAI: Human in the loop
Arize: What Is Human-On-The-Loop?

cards.title: AI apps earn 41% more per payer, then lose them faster

visual.title: Annual subscribers still paying after a year, RevenueCat

cards.what: RevenueCat data shows AI apps earn $30.16 per payer in year one, against $21.37. Only 21.1% of annual subscribers stay.
cards.why: AI helps sell the first subscription. It does not yet keep the customer, and every use has a cost.
cards.say: Pick one app. Measure who is still active in month two before adding any AI feature.
deeper: The figures come from RevenueCat's 2026 State of Subscription Apps report, built on more than 115,000 apps. AI apps also convert trials to paid at 8.5%, against 5.6% for others. So the front of the funnel is strong. The weakness appears later: 21.1% annual retention against 30.7%.

For a solo builder, that points to where effort pays. A sharper paywall adds little if the habit is missing. Decide what a user should come back for each week, build that first, and treat the AI feature as a reason to stay, not just a reason to try.

blocks.sub: One line to raise with a leader

question.text: If a critical supplier lost its chief executive tonight, which of our programmes would slip first?
question.context: Prompted by Nvidia. Most risk registers rank suppliers by spend. Few rank them by how much of the roadmap depends on one firm's delivery, pricing or leadership.
